common_name: Morris Clint's Rain Lily (Blush-Pink Spring-Flowering Natural Hybrid Species)

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in gritty, fast-draining soil in early spring; this naturally occurring cross of two Mexican rain lily species opens its cupped, blush-pink flowers in flushes after spring rains rather than on a single fixed schedule.

directions: This species arose naturally where the ranges of Zephyranthes drummondii and Zephyranthes lindleyana overlap in northern Mexico, and it combines the flat, glossy foliage of one parent with the soft pink, upward-facing cups of the other. Grow it in lean, gritty soil with sharp drainage, since standing winter moisture is the most common cause of bulb loss in this hybrid complex. Flowering begins as early as April and repeats through spring and into summer whenever rainfall follows a dry spell, so gardeners can mimic this with a deep watering during dry stretches. Established clumps are long-lived and slowly bulk up without division for many years.

common_name: Jones's Rain Lily (Texas Endemic Afternoon-Blooming Fragrant Rain Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in sandy loam in full sun; this coastal-bend Texas endemic is a naturally occurring hybrid between a night-blooming and a day-blooming rain lily, which is why its fragrant flowers open specifically in the afternoon.

directions: Native only to a handful of counties around Victoria and Refugio on the Texas coastal bend, this globally vulnerable rain lily is a stabilized natural hybrid between the night-blooming Zephyranthes chlorosolen and a day-blooming Habranthus, which explains its unusual afternoon flowering window. Each glossy, rounded-leaved bulb sends up fragrant blooms from midsummer into early fall, opening dark yellow with a brownish exterior on the first day and fading to soft creamy yellow on the second. Give it sandy, well-drained soil that dries between waterings, since this species evolved in open swales and ditches that flood briefly and then dry out quickly. Because wild populations are restricted and threatened, source bulbs only from nurseries propagating known garden-origin stock rather than wild-collected material.

common_name: Showy Rain Lily (Sunny Cadmium-Yellow Texas Gulf Coast Species)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in low, seasonally moist ground in full sun; this Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast native comes from wet roadside ditches and coastal prairies and tolerates periodic flooding better than most rain lily species.

directions: Collected originally from wet coastal prairie near Refugio, Texas, this species produces an abundance of bright, crocus-like cadmium-yellow flowers held just above grassy, glossy foliage. Unlike many drought-adapted rain lilies, it comes from seasonally flooded low ground, so it tolerates and even prefers soil that stays evenly moist through the growing season rather than baking dry. Foliage grows through the cooler months and dies back in summer heat, with the flush of flowers arriving in autumn a few days after rain. The species reproduces apomictically, so seed-grown offsets come true to the parent plant, making it easy to bulk up a planting from a single clump.

common_name: Refugio Rain Lily (Texas Gulf Coast Highway-Median Yellow Species)

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; this Refugio County, Texas endemic naturally grows in roadside ditches and highway medians and is exceptionally tough once its clumps are established.

directions: Named for the roadside ditches around Refugio, Texas where it was first documented, this rain lily is closely related to and often confused with Zephyranthes pulchella but forms slower-multiplying, longer-lived clumps. Glossy green foliage sets off bright yellow, goblet-shaped flowers that appear from late summer into fall, typically within a few days of a soaking rain. It tolerates the mowing and periodic disturbance of roadside habitat, which makes it forgiving of casual garden care once bulbs are established. Plant in full sun with good drainage and allow clumps to remain undisturbed for years, since flowering improves as the colony thickens.
